newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa says Mideast arms deals endangered by leak.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa says Mideast arms deals endangered by leak.

text.p: Two of the biggest arms deals South Africa has ever negotiated are in jeopardy after newspapers named the prospective Middle Eastern buyers, Pretoria's Defence Minister Joe Modise said on Thursday.
He and top defence industry officials acknowledged that two major deals were under discussion, but said they could not give details as the clients had requested confidentiality.
South African papers reported recently that Saudi Arabia was negotiating to buy missiles and G6 self-propelled howitzers in a sale worth some seven billion rand ($1.5 billion).
"I am worried about this deal, whether it is going to go through. I took part in the promotion of that sale," Modise told a news conference, without naming Saudi Arabia.

State arms maker Denel, which used to sell its wares clandestinely to bypass anti-apartheid sanctions, said on Thursday that it would stop trying to block the naming of the country as it had already appeared widely in print.
Local newspapers say Denel is also close to a deal to sell Kuwait 100 G5 and G6 howitzers, worth some four billion rand.
Denel did not threaten to use the same apartheid-era secrecy law it invoked in the Saudi case to stop Kuwait being named, but the defence minister said it could also be detrimental.
"I think we are going to lose that deal too," Modise warned in an apparent reference to the Kuwait negotiations.
He said buyers in both deals had demanded confidentiality that had been breached by the leak to the press.
"I don't know what they are going to say now," he said. He was asked to say if there had been any complaints or threats to pull out from the deals, but gave no details.
White-ruled South Africa built up a formidable industry to equip its army after U.N. sanctions stopped it buying freely overseas.
President Nelson Mandela, who came to power in 1994's first all-race elections, imposed restrictions on sales to countries in crisis areas or with poor human rights records.
Planned sales to Syria -- stalled after U.S. complaints -- as well as to Turkey and Rwanda have sparked fierce criticism.
Modise, who warned South Africa's self-imposed restrictions were severely hurting the defence industry, said he would visit the countries involved in the latest two deals to intercede.
"I'm going there to plead, I'm going to go down on my knees," he said. "But my chances are very slim."
Ron Haywood, executive chairman of state arms procurement and export promotion agency Armscor, told Reuters the deals were crucial to the arms industry but could still proceed.
"I'd like to be optimistic...that the chances are we could well still be back in place but it is requiring a lot of extra effort from our minister," he said.
"He's been given an unnecessary task to do on a deal which was all but properly signed off."

Presenting Armscor's annual report with Modise, he said South Africa's arms exports faced tough competition but were still worth about one billion rand a year, second only to the motor industry in terms of manufactured exports.
This equals about half a percent of the world arms trade that is dominated by the United States.
